title: Visit payload for a partner
prompt: A partner API takes each visit as one line of JSON. Write `solve(encounters)` so every visit comes back with that JSON text.
rules: The JSON object has the keys `class` (from `encounter_class`), `vitals` and `codes`, in that order.

`vitals` holds `heart_rate`, `systolic` and `diastolic` only, in that order. A visit with no vitals has no `vitals` key at all. A visit with vitals keeps the key even when every reading in it is missing.
`codes` is the number of entries in `diagnosis_codes`: 0 for an empty list, and no `codes` key when the list itself is missing. Missing readings have no key either.
hints: `F.to_json` writes a struct as JSON text and leaves out every field that is missing.
So the difference between no `vitals` key and `"vitals":{}` is the difference between a missing struct and a struct of missing values.
Keep the existing struct and remove the temperature with `F.col("vitals").dropFields("temperature_c")`; rebuilding it with `F.struct` turns a missing struct into an empty one.
starter:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F


def solve(encounters):
    # Return encounter_id and the visit as JSON text.
    return encounters
explanation: Build one struct and write it with `to_json`: `F.to_json(F.struct(F.col("encounter_class").alias("class"), F.col("vitals").dropFields("temperature_c").alias("vitals"), F.size("diagnosis_codes").alias("codes")))`. `to_json` leaves out missing fields, so the result depends on what is missing. `dropFields` keeps a missing `vitals` missing, so a telehealth visit has no `vitals` key, while a struct whose readings are all missing still prints as `{}`. `F.struct("vitals.heart_rate", ...)` would build a struct for every visit and print `"vitals":{}` for telehealth. `F.size` of a missing list is missing, so that key disappears too, while an empty list gives `0`.
